World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: How a Vietnamese bakery became a staple in Sydney's Little India
World.content:
On a strip of Indian businesses in Sydney's Harris Park, a Vietnamese bakery has outlived numerous restaurants and grocers in a suburb that is defined by its South Asian offerings.

Kevin Bui has served baked goods for more than three decades on the corner of Wigram Street in Harris Park, known fondly as Little India.

"When we first came here, [the area was] Filipino, and after that it was Greek, and then Lebanese … and then the Indians came over," Mr Bui said.

He has seen the suburb take shape over recent years.

"At first, I was worried if the business would collapse," the bakery owner said.

" And then a few customers came to me, and they asked for the buns … and they liked it. "

Keeping the bakery afloat in the heart of Harris Park took quick-thinking from its shop owner. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

An Indian street food staple

The business, Jason King's Bakery, survived the Indian retail growth in Harris Park with a steady flow of demand from restaurants and street food vendors.

What Mr Bui sold as a "soft bun", many South Asian business owners called a "pav" or "dabeli bun".

The soft buns from Mr Bui's bakery are used in many dishes sold by Little India's street food vendors. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The soft bread roll is a staple to any street food menu, often served with a vegetable curry or stuffed with potato and chutney.

"Blacktown and Bella Vista, everywhere, all the restaurants from Pendle Hill, St Marys, they buy the buns from me," Mr Bui said.

Mr Bui's weekends are the busiest, where he starts work at about 8pm and bakes until the morning, producing thousands of buns.

" [My wife] looks after the big customers and the payments. Me? I only look after the dough and the flour. "

The bakery produces thousands of buns on weekends. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Lebanese sweet shop adapts to survive

Diagonally across the road from the bakery is one of the only other non-South Asian eateries on Wigram Street.

A Lebanese sweet shop has been family-owned for over three decades and survived the area's changing demographic by changing ingredients.

SweetLand Patisserie manager Anthony Elkadi said the store had to adapt when the Indian population boomed.

"The majority of them are vegetarian, and they don't have egg, and what we did is we've created a cake without egg, and we've become well-known for it," he said.

SweetLand Patisserie has changed some of its recipes to cater for the demographic. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Mr Elkadi plans to take over the store from his father to keep it alive.

"It's a beautiful thing to be able to not only give sweets to the community but [also] give them that sense of having another home to be in."

Serving cakes, baklava and coffee, the patisserie has been fuelled by cake orders from Indians and regulars from the Lebanese community.

'Diverse traffic from all over Sydney'

Sanjay Deshwal spoke of the impact of Little India on Australia's South Asian community. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Sanjay Deshwal, president of the Little India Harris Park Business Precinct, said small businesses on Wigram Street brought "a large amount of foot traffic" to the area.

"The Indian grocery shops opened first, then the Indian restaurants opened, and then a lot of Indian consultancies and garment shops opened … so that brought a lot of diverse traffic from all over Sydney," Mr Deshwal said.

" Australia is like a big shock for most of the migrants … so Little India is like the first landing spot. "

Despite increasing rents as the area's property value grew, Mr Bui said the influx of Indian businesses "brought the area up".

"For me, I have to work hard, but I'm not stressed about the business … that's why I'm happy to serve the Indian community," he said.

The small businesses on Wigram Street have brought a large amount of foot traffic to the area. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Not ready to sell

Mr Bui has run the bakery with his wife, Julie Bui, for more than 30 years.

"My boy was only three [when we opened the store], he used to run around the shop," he said.

"In our culture we work for our children."

Mr Bui named the bakery after his son, Jason, which he said was a common practice back home.

Mr Bui and his wife are not yet ready to hang up the oven mitts of their bakery. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Despite offers from his customers to buy the bakery, Mr Bui was not ready to hang up the oven mitts.

"If I sell the business, I'll stay at home, and it's boring … at least here, I'm the boss, I'm happy to work," Mr Bui said with a smile.

"Most of the Indian people [in the area], they know me, I'm happy with the business, my stress is gone."

World.title: Why this man risked crocodiles, storms and jail to fish in Australian waters
World.content:
Deep inside Darwin's maximum-security prison, Indonesian fisherman Dora Hamidung recounts the horrors of fatal crocodile attacks and tropical storms on his journeys to Australia.

He is a repeat offender who has been caught fishing illegally in Australian waters 11 times over 20 years, and now he is serving a four-month jail term.

Despite the consequences, Dora says poverty has forced him to continue sailing to Australia's northern waters, in a fragile wooden boat, in search of precious seafood.

He is one of many Indonesians detained every year for illegal fishing, and wants to tell his story.

Dora's story

Last year, Dora and his crew were caught with 40 kilograms of illegally harvested sea cucumber in Rowley Shoals Marine Park off the coast of Western Australia.

At the time, his lawyer said they were repeat offenders who "should have known better", and four of them were jailed.

Native species of sea cucumber, known as trepang, are a delicacy overseas and are popular targets for Indonesian seafarers like Dora.

However, it is not a recent phenomenon, as Indonesian people have travelled to Australia for fishing and trade with First Nations groups for centuries.

Dora has been a fisherman since childhood. (Supplied: Department of Corrections)

The ABC was granted access to Darwin prison to speak to Dora, on the condition that the interview was supervised by the Department of Corrections.

Speaking through an interpreter, Dora said he was the vessel's captain, and he and his crew battled severe weather on the way to Australia.

"This trip was very dangerous because the rain was relentless … the wind and the waves were very, very high," he said.

" As fishermen, when we encounter big, strong winds, a lot of us die or disappear. "

Dora and his crewmates fished illegally from a 12-metre wooden vessel named Julfikar. (Supplied)

Dora has been on the water since he left school in grade five, taking over the position from his father, who had just died.

"If you saw my life with my parents over there, I'm sure you would cry," Dora said.

"I also look after my mum and the house, and the wooden foundations of my house are all nearly broken."

On board the Julfikar, authorities discovered 40 kilograms of trepang, fishing gear, and salt used to preserve the catch. (Supplied)

This year alone, border authorities have intercepted 21 illegal foreign fishing vessels and seized more than 3.5 tonnes of trepang.

A special operation was launched to deal with the problem in Queensland.

When Dora and his crew were caught last year, they stood to earn about $500 each.

Dora on the day of his most recent arrest in WA waters. (Supplied)

'A lot' of crocodiles

Dora said weather was not the only danger, and claimed he once saw a crocodile kill a crewmate near the Tiwi Islands, 80 kilometres north of Darwin.

"The crocodile grabbed my crew member's leg, and then four of us jumped on the crocodile and then I poked the crocodile's eyes," he said.

Dora said a crewmate was killed by a crocodile near the Tiwi Islands during a fishing trip in the past 12 months. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Dora said the man escaped but later died at sea, despite the crew's best efforts to save him.

The ABC could not independently verify the death, however environmental anthropologist Natasha Stacey said it was highly plausible.

Professor Stacey recently co-authored a report commissioned by the federal government to investigate why fishers like Dora continue to make the perilous journey.

"[Indonesian] people are aware that fishing is a risky business and that the benefits don't always outweigh the costs," she said.

"We did hear that some fishers had been attacked by crocodiles and that in at least one instance someone had died."

Natasha Stacey is an expert in what drives fishermen from Indonesia to illegally operate in Australian waters. (ABC Rural: Sam Parry)

She said individual reasons for illegal fishing varied, and Indonesian fishers were often mistakenly considered a "homogenous" group.

A co-dependent relationship

Professor Stacey also examined the influence of "'patron-client relationships" on illegal fishing, where boat owners offer credit in exchange for ongoing services from fishers.

"It's very difficult for members of a community or a household to get out of those situations because they're such a prevalent part of life," she said.

Professor Stacey was able to confirm Dora's trip was financed by a well-known boat owner from Pepela, a small fishing community on the island of Rote.

Traditional fishing boats in Papela port, Rote Island, Indonesia. (Supplied: Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research)

Dora said his boss had "power" over him and owned dozens of boats operating illegally in Australia.

"If the boss says go and find some trepang, I will go and find some trepang because we're just fishermen," he said.

Economic development

Professor Stacey's report recommended more Australian-led community development programs in Indonesia to address illegal fishing.

A map of the Australian Fishing Zone showing where fishing is allowed in the Timor and Arafura seas. (Supplied: Australian Fisheries Management Authority)

The Australian Fisheries Management Authority (AFMA) said it undertook a multi-faceted approach, and was using the report to inform enforcement, community engagement and diplomatic activities.

AFMA said it recognised improved livelihood options "are an important consideration", but the report "covers a wide range of issues, many of which fall outside AFMA's remit".

The ABC understands Dora will be released on May 14 and returned to Indonesia.

He believes the prospect of future trips to Australia is not entirely within his control.

World.title: Iran daily briefing: A 'yawning gulf' between Iran and US as ceasefire nears end
World.content:
Hello, ABC Middle East correspondent Matthew Doran writing to you from Jerusalem on the end of:

day 52 of the war

day 13 of the ceasefire between the US, Israel and Iran

day four of the ceasefire in Lebanon

day eight of the US blockade of Iran.

Iran war live updates: Our Americas editor answers your questions from 8:30am AEST.

Here's what you need to know today:

The Middle East ceasefire is hanging by a thread, with Iran refusing to commit to further peace talks in Pakistan in protest over what it says are US violations of the fragile truce. On Sunday, US President Donald Trump said he expected another round of negotiations in Islamabad on Monday night local time, but by Monday morning Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said there was little point in the regime joining the talks.

On Sunday, said he expected another round of negotiations in Islamabad on Monday night local time, but by Monday morning Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said there was little point in the regime joining the talks. Tehran does appear to be keeping its options open , with Reuters reporting it is considering whether to join talks on Tuesday . The initial two-week ceasefire, if it lapses after exactly a fortnight, is due to expire in the early hours of Wednesday .

, with Reuters reporting it is considering whether to join talks on . The initial two-week ceasefire, if it lapses after exactly a fortnight, is due to expire in the . Aside from the debate around the merits of further talks between the US and Iran, a yawning gulf remains between the negotiating positions of the two countries. Key issues include who gets to control the Strait of Hormuz (and barely any ships made it through the vital channel on Monday) and Iran's nuclear ambitions .

Crews have been searching parts of southern Lebanon for the remains of people killed in Israeli strikes before the ceasefire there was imposed late last week. During Israel’s bombardment of claimed Hezbollah targets across the south, and the capital Beirut, more than 2,100 people were killed . Among the dead were hundreds of civilians, including many women and children. Israel continues to occupy large tracts of land seized during its invasion of the south, which it says is in response to Hezbollah rocket fire on northern Israel.

During Israel’s bombardment of claimed Hezbollah targets across the south, and the capital Beirut, . Among the dead were hundreds of civilians, including many women and children. Israel continues to occupy large tracts of land seized during its invasion of the south, which it says is in response to Hezbollah rocket fire on northern Israel. The speaker of the Lebanese parliament, Nabih Berri (who is the chairman of the Amal movement, which has an alliance with Hezbollah), has reportedly said he was told by the US ambassador to Lebanon that Washington was trying to ensure the ceasefire in the country lasted longer than 10 days. Another round of peace talks is expected in Washington on Thursday.

Here's what all that means

At 8pm on Monday night, sirens rang out across Israel. It wasn't the usual wavering tone, rising and falling, signifying incoming missile fire.

Instead, it was a steady blast of noise reminding people to pause for a minute's silence to mark Memorial Day, which commemorates fallen Israeli soldiers and victims of terrorism.

After a sustained period of aerial barrages and the relative calm of the past fortnight, it was enough to send a chill up my spine. That was before the quick realisation that it was not a moment to rush to the shelter in the bottom of the ABC bureau in Jerusalem, and wait for the noise of explosions from interceptor missiles overhead.

But anxiety about what comes next is growing across the Middle East, as the prospect of positive developments from peace talks between the US and Iran appears to be getting fainter by the hour. There's confusion this morning about exactly what will happen in the next day or so: whether senior Iranian officials will show up for negotiations in Pakistan is chief among them.

The US President himself has fuelled some of that — telling the New York Post that his representative, Vice President JD Vance, was en route to Islamabad, while other outlets reported he hadn't boarded Air Force Two for the journey east

He's also told Bloomberg the ceasefire actually lapses on Wednesday night, Washington time, potentially giving a little bit more time for a deal, but added he's unlikely to extend the truce.

Pakistani authorities are locking down Islamabad, should there be a snap decision to hold the negotiations.

Even if the talks go ahead, there’s no guarantee of an outcome – unless there are significant concessions made by Iran on the control it's wielding over the Strait of Hormuz, and the US on its blockade of the shipping channel.

But there had been hope that the negotiations would be an opportunity to extend the fragile ceasefire for a few more days or weeks. The clock is ticking before another dangerous moment in this war, now in its eighth week.

And here's the impact on Australia

Thanks for joining me. I'll see you at the same time tomorrow.

World.title: 'It's just bulldozed through': Native title holders allege cultural sites have been destroyed by mining company
World.content:
A First Nations group on South Australia's Yorke Peninsula says a mining company has bulldozed areas of cultural significance and has started development without a formal agreement with Traditional Owners, but the company says it has "continuously engaged" with the group.

Narungga Nation Aboriginal Corporation (NNAC) told ABC News Rex Minerals, which owns the Hillside copper mine 12 kilometres south of Ardrossan, had started work without a cultural heritage plan or Indigenous benefits agreement.

NNAC's chief negotiator Garry Goldsmith said he wanted Rex Minerals to stop operations to allow for an assessment.

"We believe that their machinery is just destroying, daily, every minute of every day … our cultural heritage," Mr Goldsmith said.

Lawyers acting for NNAC have asked the federal government to intervene and issue urgent stop-work orders under the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act.

Rex Minerals is developing the Hillside copper mine on SA's Yorke Peninsula. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

The operation, which is expected to yield 75,000 tonnes of copper and 60,000 ounces of gold per year, was bought by a subsidiary of Indonesian conglomerate Salim Group in 2024.

In 2011, during the exploration phase, Rex Minerals, which was then a publicly listed company, had a formal agreement in place for the management of Narungga heritage.

The document sighted by ABC News, said that if the mine was developed, both parties — including Rex Minerals' successors — "agreed to seek" to negotiate an agreement for the protection of Narungga heritage as well as a benefits package for Narungga people.

But Mr Goldsmith said the company had pushed on without an agreement.

"Ten years ago, the mine was a long way off, so the goodwill back then may not be as current today as it was then," Mr Goldsmith said.

Rex Minerals 'continuously engaged' with Narungga people

In a statement, Rex Minerals South Australia chief executive Jason Schell pointed to the 2011 agreement, which he acknowledged primarily focused on exploration activities leading up to the mine's approval in 2014.

Jason Schell says Rex Minerals has been engaging with the Narungga people. (ABC North and West SA: Christian Cominos)

Mr Schell said that in the past 18 months, Rex Minerals had presented multiple proposals for a benefits package to the NNAC board, but they had not reached an agreement.

"This package is being negotiated in good faith and provided voluntarily despite native title over the Hillside site being extinguished," Mr Schell said.

He said the proposed agreement would "deliver significant long-term investments in education, training and direct employment outcomes".

"Rex Minerals has continuously engaged with the Narungga Nation Aboriginal Corporation," he said.

"Over the last 16 years, Rex Minerals has obtained significant input from the Narungga people on how to maximise the benefits of this important project for local Aboriginal people.

"The new agreement will also include meaningful cultural support and a Narungga Community Fund for local community projects."

But Mr Goldsmith disputed that and said the native title group had been trying to negotiate with Rex Minerals for more than a year and was concerned the company was "kicking the bucket down the road".

The Hillside copper mine is situated 12 kilometres south of Ardrossan. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"We're not looking for hand-outs," Mr Goldsmith said.

"What we are looking for from Rex is for a hand-up in regards to giving us opportunities.

"To be able to show our capabilities and our capacities as individuals, as a community, as Narungga businesses and also as native title holders."

Many artefacts 'lost or destroyed'

Hillside is set on formerly freehold farmland which means native title is "extinguished", but is still subject to conditions under the Aboriginal Heritage Act 1988 (SA).

A section of the Yorke Highway, is being relocated along with other local roads, as they have been deemed too close to what will be a 500-metre-deep open-cut and underground mine.

A part of the Yorke Highway is being relocated to keep it away from the copper mine. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

In 2014, the state government assessment noted 1,000 Aboriginal artefacts had been found during surveys of the proposed mine lease.

Rex Minerals chief executive Jason Schell said a number of Narungga cultural heritage monitors had been employed to oversee the management of those artefacts in addition to undertaking "rigorous archaeological surveys".

"This careful and deliberate approach has ensured that Aboriginal heritage sites and artefacts have been recorded and protected during exploration and development activities," he said.

Mr Goldsmith said NNAC had provided monitoring services but pulled out when negotiations stalled and Rex Minerals had since hired an independent heritage monitoring company.

"We're the elected peak body by our community to undertake our rights and interests around heritage, and I think they've totally disregarded that," Mr Goldsmith said.

Narungga man Jamie Agius was working at the site for several weeks before his employment was terminated in July 2025.

Damage to Narungga site Wombat Gully during Rex Minerals' infrastructure development for the Hillside Copper Mine. (Supplied: NNAC lawyers)

Mr Agius said he observed the clearing of culturally significant creek beds, land that represented cultural storylines and the destruction of artefacts.

Lawyers said allegations against the mining company included that it had destroyed a culturally significant area, Wombat Gully, by mistake and that many artefacts were already "lost or destroyed".

Land damage at Wombat Gully. (Supplied: NNAC lawyers)

The ABC asked Rex Minerals about the allegations.

It said it actively complied with all legal requirements under the Aboriginal Heritage Act.

'There's a lot of destruction there'

Mr Agius raised his concerns with the state government in September last year.

Rex Minerals said it had submitted an application for authorisation to disturb Aboriginal heritage in June, which would go to public consultation in 2026.

"What I want is for it to be handled correctly and managed correctly for all of the Yorke Peninsula, for all community members," Mr Agius told ABC News.

"There's a lot of destruction there.

Testing drums at the Hillside copper and gold mine. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"It does hit home when you're there for a bit and you see it.

"When you connect back with Country and come back to see it, and it's just bulldozed through.

"Some of those creek beds that we've got there, they're of great significance to some of the older people."

World.title: Group that helped find Celine Cremer plan their next missing person search
World.content:
As the sun dips between trunks of stringy eucalypts in Tasmania's north-east, Jon Edmunds and Tony Hage pull on their warmest layers and pore over a map.

The pair has spent much of the past few months in the wilderness, after signing up for the volunteer-led search for missing Belgian tourist Celine Cremer.

Belgian tourist Celine Cremer went missing in Tasmania's west while bushwalking in 2023. (Supplied)

But rather than packing up and getting on with their lives after the group helped find Ms Cremer's remains two-and-a-half years after she disappeared, they are now preparing to look for another missing person — Scottsdale man Peter Willoughby.

"The people [who organised the search for] Celine, I don't think they've realised what they've created," Mr Edmunds said.

"This thing that's going to hopefully roll on and help other people bring closure."

Tony Hage (centre) found Celine Cremer's mobile phone during the December search. (Australian Story: Morgan Timms)

While the search for Ms Cremer was gruelling and emotionally exhausting, they say it built a deep connection between many of those involved — a connection that they want to keep going.

"I just cannot extend my feelings strongly enough towards the group [of volunteers]," Mr Hage said.

" It's a real close, heartfelt group. "

Alex Smith (bottom right) was involved in the Cremer search and will also take part in looking for Peter Willoughby. (Australian Story: Morgan Timms)

"Even after the search … just catching up with people, it just felt like you were catching up with old friends, like you've known them forever," Mr Edmunds said.

Many of those involved now plan to formalise the group and initiate searches for missing people in cases where police have stepped back.

While they would initially focus on Tasmania, they want to eventually operate across the country.

Tony Hage leads small group into Tarkine rainforest to search for Celine Cremer. (Australian Story: Morgan Timms)

The ABC understands the model would be unusual in Australia, as most volunteer search groups operate only under police direction.

Mr Edmunds and Mr Hage have already been busy, in a forest reserve near Launceston in the state's north-east, preparing for their next search.

Man disappears while looking for bogged car

In October last year, Peter Willoughby had returned to Hollybank Forest Reserve looking for his bogged car, hoping to find the vehicle and retrieve it.

The 76-year-old was part of a group, including his partner Katrina Clifford, but became separated from them and was never seen again.

"I want closure," Ms Clifford said.

Ms Clifford met Peter Willoughby — "Pom" to those who knew him — when, at 19, she "went to a party at his place and never went home".

Over the next 40-odd years, they built a life in Scottsdale, where he worked in forestry, they volunteered for Meals on Wheels, and he watched her hockey matches on Saturday afternoons.

"We never had harsh words, hardly ever," she said.

"If there was something we weren't happy with, we'd always make sure we'd nutted it out before we went to bed, so we didn't go to bed angry."

Katrina Clifford's long-time partner, Peter Willoughby, has been missing since October. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

On October 1 last year, the pair were heading out to lunch for Ms Clifford's birthday, when, with a little time to kill, they drove into the Hollybank Forest Reserve to look for an old motorbike track.

But after pushing across loose gravel and fallen trees, their silver Subaru Outback station wagon became so bogged that they had to call police for help.

"They came and got us about three o'clock in the morning," Ms Clifford said.

"The policeman said to me, 'You're not going to forget this birthday.'"

She believes police also offered to pull out the car, but Mr Willoughby said he would come back later to retrieve it.

Katrina Clifford and Peter Willoughby met at a party when she was 19. (Supplied: Vicki Gibbon)

"That was one of the worst decisions he'd ever made," she said.

Partner calling out 'stopped getting a reply'

Mr Willoughby, who was going through chemotherapy, then struggled to find the bogged car.

Ms Clifford said he and a friend went in a few days later to search for it, but had no luck.

On Sunday, October 5, the pair and two friends tried again.

Katrina Clifford and Peter Willoughby were celebrating her birthday when they first ran into trouble. (Supplied: Vicki Gibbon)

Mr Willoughby was reportedly pushing ahead, confident he had figured out where it was.

"I was calling out to him, and for a long time he was answering me," Ms Clifford said.

"But then when I stopped getting a reply when I was calling out, that was when I started to get a bit a little bit concerned."

They eventually called the police.

Scottsdale man Peter Willoughby has been missing since last October. (Supplied: DPFEM)

Once they arrived, Ms Clifford said she was at a loss of what to do.

"[A policewoman] said: 'The best thing you can do is go home and wait," she said.

" I feel like I've been waiting for about six or seven months now, and I'm still just waiting. "

The new search is planned for the end of May. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Case remains open

The search for Mr Willoughby began that Sunday, but was hampered by wet, cold conditions.

Emergency services said he had worn only jeans, a jumper and sneakers and his family said he carried few items besides a blockbuster — a tool like an axe for splitting wood.

When Mr Willoughby's car was found, Ms Clifford said it was 1.3 kilometres away from where he had been so sure it was, and his last known location.

She believes the chemotherapy had weakened his bush skills and had taken a toll physically.

The police search for Peter Willoughby lasted 10 days. (ABC News: Emily JB Smith)

Ms Clifford said the last few months without him had been horrific.

One of the few bright spots has been her network of friends and family, who even set up a roster to ensure someone could always stay with her at night and drive her places.

"They've been absolutely as good as you could possibly hope for," she said.

But she still holds hope for some form of closure.

"I really would like to have something to bury or to have a memorial service of some sort, something like that," she said.

" I'd like something to be found. "

Katrina Clifford and Vicki Gibbon look at an old photo of Peter Willoughby (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Tasmania Police and other search and rescue groups spent 10 days looking for Mr Willoughby and the case remains open.

Volunteers to help with Willoughby search

In late January, Ms Clifford's sister, Vicki Gibbon, received a Facebook message from Mr Edmunds offering to help in the search for Mr Willoughby.

Sisters Katrina Clifford and Vicki Gibbon hope the new search will bring closure. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

"We checked with Katrina and she said: 'Yeah, yeah, the more searching the better,'" Ms Gibbon said.

"It's just grown since then … I'm overwhelmed at the depth of work that these searchers are doing and what's involved with this search."

The new search is planned for May 29-31.

Some of those set to take part were involved in the Celine Cremer search, but with around 35 volunteers needed in total, others will be vetted to ensure they have the skills and personality to operate safely in the bush.

Volunteers take a break at base camp in Tarkine Forest during the search for Celine Cremer. (Australian Story: Morgan Timms)

A Tasmania Police spokesperson said they supported the renewed effort, giving the group mapping details of previous searches and suggesting new areas.

They also said it could see the value of an independent group assisting in other searches in the future.

"Items and information revealed during a recent private search for Celine Cremer indicates the potential effectiveness of this approach," the police spokesperson said.

Jon Edmunds has already been scouting the area, along with Mr Hage, to prepare for the new search. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Mr Edmunds was optimistic about their chances, despite a few nerves.

"The last few days, I've felt a little bit of the weight of expectation that would be from this search," he said.

He and Mr Hage have already spent hours in the bush around Hollybank searching and familiarising themselves with the terrain.

"Four days in October," Mr Hage said, reading his log of search days from a pocket notebook.

" Three days in March. And tomorrow will be my fourth day in April. "

Tony Hage has already spent considerable time camped in the Hollybank Forest Reserve, searching for Peter Willoughby. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

They said many members of the group were just as motivated after seeing firsthand with the Celine search effort the value of helping a person's family and loved ones find answers.

"It sounds boring … randomly wandering through the bush," Mr Edmunds said.

World.title: 'It's pretty touching': Students pen postcards to thank veterans
World.content:
This Anzac Day, Van Reuben is one of thousands of children across Queensland sending postcards to former and serving Australian Defence Force members.

Using red crayons, the year 5 student adds poppies to his postcard as he talks about his dad's time in the army during the war in Afghanistan.

Van Reuben is among thousands of Queensland students who have written a postcard to a veteran. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"It makes me feel glad that he fought for all the people and for our country," Van said.

"Anzac Day is special to me because I get to commemorate all those people who fought for me and I get to commemorate my dad."

Darra State School is among 190 schools across Queensland taking part in the Returned and Services League's (RSL) Postcards of Honour program.

Loading

Connecting generations

The initiative encouraging students to connect through writing a postcard to a local veteran has been running for four years.

As part of the program, a veteran from a local sub-branch attends a school to deliver a presentation about the importance of the day and the history behind the Anzacs.

Grant Hartigan says the postcards are a "tangible token of gratitude" for veterans. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Darra RSL president Grant Hartigan toured Iraq after joining the army in 2014 as an infantryman and spoke at Darra State School this year.

What it takes to make an Anzac Day wreath A remembrance tradition that Australians have adapted to commemorate fallen soldiers has ancient Greek and Roman origins.

"Seeing some of the veterans' faces when they receive these postcards is just indescribable," he said.

"Especially when they realise kids from the local school were thankful for older Australians and veteran service. It's pretty touching.

"It really gets engagement from the younger generation where they get an opportunity to show remembrance and also give a tangible token of gratitude to servicemen and women."

The exchanging of postcards is also symbolic, mimicking the events of World War I, when frontline soldiers would send postcards home to their loved ones.

Tracy Freeman says listening to veterans like Grant Hartigan helps students learn and understand. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

It's an activity Darra State High School Principal Tracy Freeman feels have helped students connect to veterans through creativity and empathy.

"Listening to Grant really helps our children to connect with their feelings and empathise how the soldiers may have felt back in the Anzac period," she said.

"The students are able to learn, they're able to connect and they're able to show gratitude to the servicemen before us and it's just across generations."

World.title: Bus replacements mean some V/Line commuters can't get to work on time
World.content:
A couple of years back, David Oborne moved to Birregurra which is about a two-hour drive west of Melbourne.

He grew up in the region and figured he would still be able catch the train to work in Melbourne a few times a week.

On weekdays, a 6:20am bus from Birregurra gets commuters to Waurn Ponds station in time for the 7:21am V/Line train to Melbourne which arrives at Southern Cross at 8:36am.

"When it works it's great, but when it's not, it's not," Mr Oborne said.

Earlier this month — amid skyrocketing petrol prices — trains were replaced with buses for line maintenance.

The earliest replacement service does not get to the city until 10:40am.

Commuters on the Warrnambool line are now forced to either drive an hour or more to the nearest station with an earlier service — typically Wyndham Vale — or all the way to Melbourne.

"It's pretty disappointing that we haven't got that like-for-like service," Mr Oborne said.

"Fuel prices are ridiculous at the moment and for me, to fill up to drive to Melbourne and back three times a week, there's no real benefit in it … it's costing you 300-odd dollars a week."

" It's not as if we can opt out of going to work. "

V/Line trains leaving Southern Cross station have been packed during the free travel period. (ABC News: James Oaten)

Then there's the issue of getting home.

"The other day it was a nightmare," he said.

"Leaving work, you get on a 5:10 train back to Wyndham Vale and then there are not enough buses to be able to accommodate the people on that train which resulted in me getting home at quarter-to-nine at night, opposed to getting on the train and coming to Birregurra at nearly seven o'clock.

"Not being able to get home on time does make it bloody hard."

Passengers wait to board the V/Line replacement bus service at Waurn Ponds station in Geelong. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Commuters on the Warrnambool and Geelong lines have been impacted by replacement bus services from April 11 to 24 to allow for maintenance and upgrade works along the line.

It was announced last week that the Warrnambool and Colac lines replacement services would continue until May 20.

The replacement services have coincided with increased passenger numbers due to Victoria's free public transport, with many V/Line commuters complaining about overcrowding on regional services.

But lack of like-for-like replacement services — running earlier buses so passengers can reach their destination at the same time as a rail service — has become a particular cause of irritation for those on the Warrnambool line.

Some V/Line passengers taking up the free public transport offer are finding their services replaced by buses that take longer to get to their destination. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Public Transport Users Association regional spokesperson Paul Westcott said scheduled line maintenance was an "unavoidable necessity" but the lack of early replacement services was unacceptable.

"You would think it was incumbent on the V/Line to offer a like-for-like [replacement service] if a train service is cancelled for maintenance or is discontinued for a while," Mr Westcott said.

"It's just not acceptable to cancel a train or to stop running a train for maintenance and then not provide a like service with the replacement buses.

"Obviously, there are fewer public transport services in the regions so the ones that are there are very valuable, and people have to build their schedules around those relatively infrequent services."

Liberal MP Richard Riordan says regional commuters should receive the same standard of service as city users. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Polwarth state Liberal MP Richard Riordan said the lack of earlier replacement services was "simply not fair".

"Public transport and good connections from our regions into the city are vital," Mr Riordan said.

"You can't be arriving in Melbourne at lunchtime, particularly if you're elderly or disabled, and then expect to get your specialist medical appointments.

" People in Melbourne … would not cop public transport — free public transport — that didn't get you into the city until lunchtime. "

Mr Riordan called on V/Line to provide a like-for-like service for commuters affected by the Warrnambool and Colac line upgrade.

V/Line says the bus replacements allow for important rail upgrades that will improve safety and reliability for commuters. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

When asked if the replacement coach service timetable for the Warrnambool line would be updated to include earlier services, V/Line said it would review customer feedback and explore if adjustments were necessary.

"We're delivering important maintenance upgrades to the Warrnambool and Geelong lines throughout April and May to ensure the continued safety and reliability for passengers," a V/Line spokesperson said.

"We thank passengers for their patience and ask them to allow extra time to get to their destination while replacement coaches are operating."

The state government announced over the weekend that it would extend the free public transport period until the end of May.

Yesterday, it announced the 2026/27 budget would include funding for more V/Line services on the Shepparton line as well as the Belgrave, Lilydale, Glen Waverley, Alamein, Mernda and Hurstbridge lines in Melbourne.

But the full roll out may not be operational until next year.

World.title: Leave without pay, or lose your job — decision day for smelter workers
World.content:
The administrator of the Liberty Bell Bay manganese smelter in northern Tasmania is confident the underlying business is viable and a buyer will be found among the Australian and international bidders who have expressed interest.

"It's definitely a viable business," Morgan Kelly, of Ernst and Young, told the ABC.

"It's a business that's got great potential in terms of its earning capability."

" I am confident that we will achieve a sale. It's all subject to confidentiality [but] we have a mix of Australian-domiciled and international interested parties. "

The smelter is a major employer for George Town. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Mr Kelly said the bids received under the non-binding indicative offer process, which closed on Friday, were "absolutely" predicated on keeping the 216-strong workforce intact.

"There's a very strong desire to retain the full workforce," he said.

Liberty Bell Bay production manager Health Williams says government support is needed. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

"A major part of what we're selling here is we've got a really great supplier network, we've got a really great customer network, we've got an operating smelter, and we've got a fantastic workforce which is ready to return to work.

"So that's a very important part of the sale process, and a very big part of the value of [what] we're selling."

Liberty Bell Bay was placed into voluntary administration last month by private equity firm White Oak, which had been a secured lender to parent entity Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance, which collapsed last year.

Liberty Bell Bay enters voluntary administration The owner of Australia's only manganese alloy smelter has entered voluntary administration. It means further uncertainty for the Tasmanian smelter's workforce.

Mr Kelly said Liberty Bell Bay had been cash-starved under the ownership of GFG.

"It's really a question of capital constraint rather than anything else, which has caused challenges for this business, and that's impacting us in the administration process as well."

On Thursday, the administrators EY told workers there was no more money to continue paying wages beyond this week and about 175 would be faced with the choice of taking leave without pay or facing redundancy.

Those have been given until the end of today to make a decision.

Workers have been given until today to decide if they will take leave without pay, or lose their job. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Mr Kelly declined to say what proportion of the workforce would choose to go unpaid, but said the main objective of administrators was to keep the workforce "intact".

"We're [making] some adjustments to the workforce to allow us more time to be able to continue very limited operations while we move through phase two due diligence, but we're confident that those workforce changes will be temporary," Mr Kelly said.

"Our main objective is to keep the workforce intact.

"We're just trying to make it as short a period of time as humanly possible that anyone's without pay, but at the same time trying to keep everybody or keep the workforce available because it's a workforce with a highly specialised skill set, which is critical to this asset," he said.

Hundreds of Liberty Bell Bay workers and their families turned out to Monday's event. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Mr Kelly said he could not put a definite timeframe on the next phase of the sale process, which is conducting due diligence on the bidders, but said site inspections were being scheduled this week and he was "hoping to be well advanced within the next three to four weeks."

Smelter workers plead for government support as final payday looms Tasmanian smelter workers at risk of losing their salaries are pleading with the state and federal governments to step in — pointing to large bailouts given to other companies.

Hundreds of workers and their families attended a rally in George Town on Monday, at which union leaders and politicians spoke in support of the workforce and called for state and federal governments to intervene.

Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone chief executive Susie Bower said administrators had indicated two to six weeks of bridging funds were needed until a new buyer could be brought in.

" I think that is kind of optimistic from a due diligence point of view, but if the administrators can make it work, then let's make it work. "

Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone CEO Susie Bower says administrators had indicated two to six weeks of bridging funds were needed. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The AWU estimates the weekly wages bill at Liberty Bell Bay is $1.6 million and Chris Donovan, assistant national secretary, said only $5 million was needed to cover workers until a sale is finalised.

"When you look at the hundreds of millions of dollars, and in some cases billions of dollars, that other state and federal government have put into smelters that have run into trouble, this five million dollars is a measly amount," Mr Donovan said.

Chris Donovan, assistant national secretary of the Australian Workers' Union, spoke at Monday's rally. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Nothing 'concrete' from governments

Mr Kelly said the administrators had "very positive" discussions with both the state and federal government and had "strong indications of support".

However, he said, "we haven't had any offers [or] any discussions around anything concrete."

Tasmanian infrastructure minister Kerry Vincent said yesterday a proposal for a support package had been put to the federal government and he expected quick progress, but couldn't say when a resolution will come.

"There is a package being put forward to the federal government to assist the workers and community and we'll continue to have talks to the federal government," Mr Vincent said.

Liberty Bell Bay smelter workers are facing an uncertain future. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Federal Bass MP Jess Teesdale told the rally she was pleased to hear the Tasmanian Government had put a support package proposal to the Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres.

Smelter workers told to take leave without pay or be sacked About 175 workers at Australia's only manganese smelter, Liberty Bell Bay, have been told they will be laid off at the end of next week unless they take leave without pay.

"There are a lot of potential buyers in the wings here, and we just need to make sure that the actual value of that facility, which is its people, are there for that sale," she said.

A spokesperson for federal industry minister Tim Ayres said the workforce was facing "unacceptable uncertainty" after being let down by GFG.

"The administrators, who are funded by White Oak, are pursuing a rapid sales process for the assets," they said.

"The Liberty Bell Bay workforce is a core part of the value of that sale and must be recognised and treated as such throughout the process.

"The Australian government has worked and is continuing to work closely with the Tasmanian Government to ensure workers and local suppliers are supported and receive appropriate assistance."

Heath Williams had support from his kids at the rally. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Workers nervous, but hopeful

Generations of George Town families have worked at the smelter and local businesses and schools would suffer if it never reopened.

Liberty Bell Bay production manager Health Williams said the smelter was a profitable business with "the right owner".

"I'm hoping that the government will lend a lot of support to get it in the right hands because that's what it needs," he said.

Attending this morning, Mr Williams said he was nervous, but hopeful of a positive outcome.

EY's Mr Kelly told the ABC that, including all off-balance sheet liabilities, the liability to employee creditors was about $34 million and there was in excess of $20 million owed to unsecured creditors.

"We've only had the first meeting of creditors and we haven't called for proofs of debt or adjudicated on those yet, and I haven't even talked about the inter-company loans, which are very complicated," he said.

World.title: Property bloom: Construction set to begin on West End tower at site of former florist
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane development Property bloom: Construction set to begin on West End tower at site of former florist William Davis April 21, 2026 — 6:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Construction of an apartment block will begin in the middle of this year on the site of a former flower shop in a booming pocket of West End. The Elisi building at 17 Ferry Road – previously occupied by the Roses Only warehouse – will comprise 30 three-bedroom units across eight storeys. The now vacant block at 17 Ferry Road in West End where the Elisi building will be erected. William Davis A pool, barbecue area and yoga lawn will be included on the roof. Each apartment will have an outdoor area and two underground parking spaces. The former flower shop and car park has already been demolished. Brisbane Times confirmed construction would begin in July, and was expected to be finished in late 2027.



It’s a booming area of West End, next to the enormous The Lanes Montague Markets project and directly opposite a planned apartment building at 24 Ferry Road. Sales agent Doug Tonkin said buyers were being drawn to the area due to its proximity to city services, Orleigh Park, and West End State School and Brisbane State High School. “It’s an overcrowded market, you’ve got a lot of high density popping up ... so to do something with only 30 apartments, we feel there is definitely a market for it,” he said. “When we look at the demographics, we’re really plugging into downsizers … people that are coming out of leafy suburbs of Brisbane.”



The apartments are priced between $1,799,000 and $2,209,000, with four different layouts offered. Tonkin said about 12 had been sold. An artist impression of Elisi at 17 Ferry Road in West End. Prospect Rapid development in the area has faced criticism from some locals, who believe population growth is rapidly outstripping services. West End Community Association president Seleneah More said in 2025 the whole suburb was already struggling to keep up. “The infrastructure we need, they just haven’t put in place to deal with that growth.

World.title: ‘Hit piece’: FBI director sues over article portraying him as MIA, problem drinker
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS politics ‘Hit piece’: FBI director sues over article portraying him as MIA, problem drinker Michael Koziol April 21, 2026 — 5:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Washington: FBI director Kash Patel is suing The Atlantic magazine over an explosive article that portrayed him as “missing in action” and a problem drinker whose behaviour has alarmed those around him at the nation’s top crime-fighting agency. The article, published on Friday, said multiple witnesses described Patel’s “bouts of excessive drinking”, and reported that there was widespread concern in the US government about his conspicuous intoxication. FBI director Kash Patel is suing The Atlantic magazine over an article portraying him as unreliable and a problem drinker. Bloomberg Multiple times in the past year, members of Patel’s security detail “had difficulty waking [him] because he was seemingly intoxicated”, The Atlantic reported, citing “information supplied to Justice Department and White House officials”. The magazine alleged that at one point, staff made a request for “breaching equipment” – ramming gear used by SWAT and hostage teams to enter buildings – because Patel was unreachable behind a locked door.



Patel’s colleagues are reportedly concerned his behaviour has become a threat to public safety, and that he may be missing or unavailable while the nation responds to a domestic terrorist attack. A Donald Trump loyalist and a national security official during the first Trump administration, Patel was appointed by the president in part to reform the FBI after what both men believe was the politicisation and weaponisation of the agency under Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden. In the lawsuit, filed in the US District Court for the District of Columbia on Monday morning (US time), Patel’s lawyers said The Atlantic article constituted a “sweeping, malicious, and defamatory hit piece” that crossed a legal line and contained “false and obviously fabricated allegations”. The journalist, Sarah Fitzpatrick, “could not get a single person to go on the record in defence of these outrageous allegations”, the complaint said, and instead relied on anonymous sources “she knew to be both highly partisan with an axe to grind and also not in a position to know the facts”.



Patel also accused the magazine of a “well-documented, long-running editorial animus” against him, failing to give him enough time to respond to their questions and “deliberately structuring the pre-publication process to avoid receiving information that would refute their narrative”. The Atlantic said in a statement that it stood by its reporting and would vigorously defend itself and Fitzpatrick against the “meritless lawsuit”. Oil prices are climbing following the latest rise of tensions between the United States and Iran, but the moves are more modest than they were earlier in the war. US stocks, meanwhile, are giving back a bit of their record-breaking rally. The S&P 500 slipped 0.4 per cent from its all-time high and is on track for just its second drop in 14 days after the United States seized an Iranian-flagged cargo vessel that it said had tried to evade its blockade of Iranian ports. The Dow Jones was down 109 points, or 0.2 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.5 per cent lower. Wall Street is in the red to start the week. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.78¢. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, climbed 5.4 per cent to $US95.28 on worries that Iran could keep petroleum pent up in the Persian Gulf if it continues to block tankers from exiting the Strait of Hormuz.



It’s a turnaround from the last trading day on Wall Street, when stocks soared and oil prices tumbled Friday after Iran said it was reopening the strait to commercial traffic. Construction of an apartment block will begin in the middle of this year on the site of a former flower shop in a booming pocket of West End. The Elisi building at 17 Ferry Road – previously occupied by the Roses Only warehouse – will comprise 30 three-bedroom units across eight storeys. The now vacant block at 17 Ferry Road in West End where the Elisi building will be erected. William Davis A pool, barbecue area and yoga lawn will be included on the roof. Each apartment will have an outdoor area and two underground parking spaces. The former flower shop and car park has already been demolished. Brisbane Times confirmed construction would begin in July, and was expected to be finished in late 2027.



It’s a booming area of West End, next to the enormous The Lanes Montague Markets project and directly opposite a planned apartment building at 24 Ferry Road. The apartments are priced between $1,799,000 and $2,209,000, with four different layouts offered. Tonkin said about 12 had been sold. An artist impression of Elisi at 17 Ferry Road in West End. West End Community Association president Seleneah More said in 2025 the whole suburb was already struggling to keep up. “The infrastructure we need, they just haven’t put in place to deal with that growth.

Washington: FBI director Kash Patel is suing The Atlantic magazine over an explosive article that portrayed him as “missing in action” and a problem drinker whose behaviour has alarmed those around him at the nation’s top crime-fighting agency. The article, published on Friday, said multiple witnesses described Patel’s “bouts of excessive drinking”, and reported that there was widespread concern in the US government about his conspicuous intoxication. Bloomberg Multiple times in the past year, members of Patel’s security detail “had difficulty waking [him] because he was seemingly intoxicated”, The Atlantic reported, citing “information supplied to Justice Department and White House officials”. The magazine alleged that at one point, staff made a request for “breaching equipment” – ramming gear used by SWAT and hostage teams to enter buildings – because Patel was unreachable behind a locked door.



Patel’s colleagues are reportedly concerned his behaviour has become a threat to public safety, and that he may be missing or unavailable while the nation responds to a domestic terrorist attack. World.title: AI tells tenant she should ask for $40,000 - tribunal hands her $80
World.content:
Photo: RNZ

Tenants using artificial intelligence to help them make applications to the Tenancy Tribunal are creating extra work and backlog, one property manager says.

Property Brokers general manager of property management David Faulkner said there had been a noticeable shift towards AI-written applications that tended to be longer, more complex and sometimes claiming excessive amounts of money.

He said his firm received a notice of hearing for a tenancy dispute just before Christmas. A tenant had claimed that she and her child had their safety compromised when they were renting a rural property with unsafe drinking water.

"There were other issues as well - a claim of retaliatory notice, breaches of quiet enjoyment, and a dryer breaking down, which took a total of four weeks to repair. Her claim was for $40,000.

"What we received was a total of 215 pages, made up of the application, evidence, photographs, and a 101 page written report outlining the claim and breaking down the costs that should be awarded to her. The basis of the claim was that the pH level of the water was at a level that made it dangerous to drink. There were two hearings, one remote and one in person.

"On 2 April, the adjudicator published the Tribunal order. The tenant was awarded a grand total of $80 for the inconvenience of the dryer."

He said excessively long, seemingly AI-generated claims like this put pressure on staff as well as the owners of the property.

"[That] was probably the first one, and we're thinking this looks very, very complex. Then you start to see two or three more come through asking for really big amounts, $40,000, $50,00, $60,000 and they're all set out in the same format. It just becomes quite clear that it's AI-generated.

"A tenant may have a grievance, they put it together, and, you know, in good old days they'd probably go to somebody like a tenancy union or a tenant advocate, and at least could have a conversation with them, but AI in some cases is just giving them information which is just not being verified. And they're probably getting very excited about what they think they can get, and they submit it in. And it's started to cause a few problems."

He said Tenancy Tribunal adjudicators were having to go through all the pages of evidence and it slowed the process.

Faulkner said some claims did not have merit and others were exorbitant.

Landlords submit the bulk of Tenancy Tribunal applications, commonly for rent arrears. Faulkner said these cases often did not need to be dealt with via a hearing and the tribunal could speed up the rate at which it heard cases by dealing with hem remotely.

Sarina Gibbon, director at Tenancy Advisory, said it was true that cases were being lodged that were more complex and sometimes meritless.

But she said it was probably another stage in the evolution of technology.

Photo: Supplied

"If you look at the overall system in terms of the common challenges we have now which is to make the tribunal pipeline flow more effectively and minimise wait time so genuine applications are not having to wait months and months and months to get a hearing, in that sense having a very primitive grasp of AI is not helping.

"But if you take a step back and consider the overall intent of a tenancy-specific tribunal, which is really set up to promote cheap and expedited justice or dispute resolution … if AI enables more applicants to put forward applications, is that helpful? Yeah, I think it's helpful. It's serving justice and giving access to justice to more people.

"I don't see a problem with AI as such, I think this is a reflection of simply that the technology is just so new and we're still such naive and primitive users that we're grasping with what this technology means. So right now what is happening is a lot of people are engaging with AI with very little knowledge of the RTA themselves. So they're buying into AI hallucination, they're buying into this tremendous amount of bloat that AI produces.

"I'm a lover of technology, over time I'm confident that AI is going to get us to a point where it's going to be, it's going to be a help rather than a hindrance."

It comes after the Insurance and Financial Services Ombudsman warned last week that people should fact-check the information AI was giving them when they made complaints.

In one example seen by the IFSO Scheme, a Google AI summary suggested that insurance claim decisions are "frequently overturned" when consumers complained, and that "up to 80 or 90 percent of cases can result in success if people persist".

But Insurance and Financial Services Ombudsman Karen Stevens said that was misleading.

She said complaints that escalated were often complex and stressful, and not always able to be resolved in the consumer's favour.

She said AI responses could make the process more frustrating for people when reality did not match their expectations.

"While AI can be very useful for general information, it can sometimes oversimplify complex policy wording, miss key exclusions, and rely on overseas information that doesn't apply in New Zealand. We've also seen instances of AI hallucinating previous cases and using them as examples. This can result in it giving incorrect advice," she said.

"We've seen complaints which are 300 pages long. But more words aren't necessarily better. Clear information about what has gone wrong for someone is much more useful than multiple pages referencing legislation and case law."

World.title: Indian community welcomes ‘momentous’ free trade deal
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Marika Khabazi

New Zealand's Indian community has welcomed the government's decision to sign a long-awaited free trade agreement with India next week in New Delhi, describing it as a major milestone in bilateral trade ties.

Trade Minister Todd McClay has confirmed that legal verification of the agreement has been completed, with both governments set to formally sign the deal on 27 April.

Negotiations concluded in December last year.

The government says the agreement will eliminate or reduce tariffs on 95 percent of New Zealand exports to India, one of the highest levels secured in any Indian trade deal.

The signing will now trigger a parliamentary process, with the full text and a national interest analysis to be submitted and reviewed by a select committee, alongside public submissions.

Business and community leaders say the deal has been a long time coming, potentially unlocking significant economic opportunities.

That said, some are urging caution around implementation and migration safeguards.

Photo: Supplied / New Zealand Indian Central Association

Veer Khar, president of the New Zealand Indian Central Association, said he remained confident the deal would ultimately gain cross-party backing.

"It's an election year, so we understand political parties will make the most of the opportunity to take shots at each other and that's fair and part of the process," he said.

"But ultimately, we're confident the deal will be signed because it offers so much benefit."

Photo: Blessen Tom

Sudesh Jhunjhnuwala, chief executive of Sudima Hotels and Hind Management, described the agreement as a "once in a lifetime deal".

Having been part of the prime minister's delegation last year, he said India's renewed interest in an FTA with New Zealand came as a surprise.

He added that establishing direct flight connections would be a natural next step.

"Whenever there's a direct flight, tourism from India takes off, and at the same time it will send more tourists to India as well," he said.

Jhunjhnuwala said stronger economic conditions driven by the FTA would also support domestic tourism.

"The exciting part about the FTA is that it brings economic benefits to New Zealand, he said.

"And when the economy is doing well, people spend more locally. Over 50 percent of our business comes from domestic tourism."

Photo: RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Dame Ranjna Patel said the level of public debate around the agreement was disproportionate.

"When New Zealand signed the China free trade deal there wasn't this much kerfuffle," she said.

"We're a very small cog in the system, and I don't know what fearmongering is about the FTA. It's such a good thing to happen."

She said the political noise could be related to the upcoming election.

"We probably won't get a second chance if we turn it down right now," she said.

Photo: Supplied

Sunil Kaushal, chief executive of the India New Zealand Business Council, called the signing "a momentous occasion" that had been decades in the making.

"It's been a long time coming," he said. "As the good old Mainland Cheese ad would say, 'good things take time'."

Kaushal said he believed Parliament would ultimately support the agreement.

"I think Labour will make the best decision for the country rather than the party because this deal will add more jobs and more money into the economy," he said.

Arunima Dhingra, chief executive of immigration and education agency Aims Global, welcomed the signing but said attention must now turn to outcomes.

"For years we've talked about the potential, and now we're keen to see what it actually delivers," Dhingra said.

She said the agreement could strengthen collaboration in education, skilled talent and investment.

"There are parts of India that are world-leading at the moment," she said.

"Better partnership and alignment could allow New Zealand to test ideas on a much larger global stage."

Dhingra emphasised the need to focus on skilled migration.

Kush Bhargava, chief executive of the Aotearoa Bharat Economic Foundation, said the deal would boost New Zealand businesses by improving direct links with India and reducing tariffs, calling it a potential "game changer".

Manu Lambai, manager of Indian jewellery giant Malabar Gold and Diamonds' Auckland showroom, said the deal would also expand access to specialised products in New Zealand.

"Those who make these kinds of specialised, handcrafted jewellery are in India, and with the FTA we can bring them directly to New Zealand," Lambai said.

The company entered the New Zealand market following the country's comprehensive economic partnership agreement with the United Arab Emirates.

Photo: RNZ / Blessen Tom

Mahesh Muralidhar, chief executive of Phase One Ventures and National Party candidate for Tāmaki, said the agreement would open up new opportunities.

"India is one of the fastest-growing economies in the world and will maintain that growth for many years," he said.

"There is a highly engaged middle class that is growing rapidly and will demand more services, products and food."

He said New Zealand was well placed to meet that demand through innovation and expertise, and that the deal would also hold significance for the Indian diaspora.

Photo: RNZ / Angus Dreaver

Labour MP for Maungakiekie Priyanca Radhakrishnan said any agreement must serve New Zealand's long-term interests, raising concerns that still needed addressing.

"Labour has raised a number of concerns about the free trade agreement that still need to be clarified by the government," she said.

"This includes wanting stronger safeguards against the exploitation of Indian migrants who come here for study, like we saw not long ago."

She said Labour would review the full details before deciding whether to support the legislation.

"Signing a free trade agreement if you don't have the majority support in Parliament - and, at this point, they don't - is irresponsible and could damage our international reputation," she said.

Photo: RNZ / Jane Patterson

Mahesh Bindra, former New Zealand First MP and chair of the New Zealand Bharat Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said the agreement would be "tremendously beneficial" but acknowledged debate was inevitable.

He said he understood concerns raised by Foreign Minister Winston Peters around immigration settings.

"His view that immigration should not be treated as an opportunity to bring in people we don't need has some merit," Bindra said.

"New Zealand needs migrants, but we need skilled migrants that the country requires, not mass migration or people using New Zealand as a stepping stone to other countries."

ACT MP Parmjeet Parmar said a free trade deal with India is an exciting prospect for both New Zealand and the Indian community.

"Such opportunities go beyond individual benefit," she said.

"Increased trade enables businesses to grow, lowers costs and opens new markets for Kiwi exporters, supporting jobs, lifting incomes and creating opportunities across the country."
